newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss polls show solid support for huge aid fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss polls show solid support for huge aid fund.

text.p: Three weekend opinion polls showed Swiss voters back a huge new humanitarian fund despite right-wing opposition to efforts to appease critics of Switzerland's financial role during the Holacaust.

Two polls published by Sunday newspapers and another from Saturday showed support between 50 and 73 percent for the government proposal for a foundation to aid the world's poor and persecuted, including survivors of Nazi genocide.

The foundation is separate from an aid fund for impoverished Holocaust survivors set up last month by Berne and Jewish groups with 265 million Swiss francs ($179.4 million) from Swiss banks, businesses and the central bank.

But the foundation plan, which would use seven billion Swiss francs in official gold reserves as capital to run the operation, is another step in Swiss efforts to answer charges by Jewish critics that it profited cynically from World War Two.
The proposed foundation was opposed by 19 to 33 percent of those surveyed since it was unveiled on Wednesday.
The Swiss cabinet voiced relief at the first sign of broad popular support after an initial wave of criticism led by far-right politicians suggested that the idea could be shot down in a referendum.

"This is a pleasant surprise. This result demonstrates a very widespread willingness among the Swiss people to support solidarity," government spokesman Achille Casanova told the newspaper Berner Zeitung.

The Berne daily's poll found 50 percent of those surveyed favoured the foundation idea. The rate of approval was 58 percent in the Sunday weekly SonntagsBlick and 73 percent in a poll comissioned by the weekly SonntagsZeitung.

President Arnold Koller proposed the "Swiss Foundation for Solidarity" in a bid to restore Switzerland's reputation after months of battering on the world stage by critics who said the country abused its neutrality by trading with Nazi Germany and turning away jewish refugees.
Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger said the foundation would reconfirm Switzerland's identity as a humanitarian country.

"This is a revival of the strengths that have always shaped Switzerland," he said. Berne has drawn parallels between the new foundation and the Swiss-run International Committee of the Red Cross started in 1863 by Geneva businessman Henry Dunant.

The foundation is meant to divide roughly 350 million Swiss francs in yearly income, expected from investing its starting capital half and half between Swiss and foreign causes. Berne must still work out the details of the foundation's focus.

Opposition to the idea has been led by far-right politicians such as industrialist and parliament member Christoph Blocher, who said the cabinet had "lost its head". Blocher has hinted he might seek a referendum against any government spending for Holocaust survivors.
The surveys were in sharp contrast to a telephone poll by the tabloid newspaper Blick published on Friday.
Under the banner headline "No!", the tabloid said 90 percent of nearly 4,000 callers had denounced the plan as a waste of Swiss central bank gold reserves.
